source.title: Predictable Scale: Part I, Step Law -- Optimal Hyperparameter Scaling Law in Large Language Model Pretraining
source.authors: Houyi Li; Wen-Zheng Zheng; Qiu-Feng Wang; Han-Shan Zhang; Zi-Li Wang; Shijie Xuyang; Yuantao Fan; Zhenyu Ding; Haoying Wang; Ning Ding; Shuigeng Zhou; Xiangyu Zhang; Da-Xin Jiang

record.file_problem: The full paper is present, though some figures and table content are garbled in the extracted text.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether architectural shape changes loss at a fixed parameter count, using controlled training experiments rather than the original loss-scaling measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper primarily studies learning-rate and batch-size scaling, not loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute, nor compute-optimal parameter-token allocation. The relevant results are its architecture-variation experiments and reported minimum-loss ranges. Hyperparameter-law comparisons and the predicted hyperparameter values do not directly test the claim versions.
record.test_reason: Appendix A.2 holds N ≈ 4.29×10^8 and D = 8B tokens fixed, varies dmodel, dff, Nhead and Nlayer across eight shapes, and compares the minimum loss after tuning LR and BS. This bears directly on V4. The paper's main subject, scaling laws for optimal learning rate and batch size, does not test V1–V3 or V5–V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The authors' main conclusion is the Step Law: optimal LR is a power law in N and D, and optimal BS depends mainly on D. Its predicted hyperparameters land within 0.094% of the grid-search optimum loss, and it generalises across shapes, MoE sparsity and data recipes. The parameter-count-versus-compute point the record leads with is a secondary appendix finding.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses controlled architecture-variation and hyperparameter-grid-search experiments to examine shape invariance; it does not reproduce the original parameter/token/compute loss-scaling or compute-optimal-allocation procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that changing the final learning-rate schedule changes the optimal learning-rate/batch-size region: a fixed final learning rate of 10−5 versus lrmin = lrmax/10 produces different optima.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed compute per token (M ≈ 2.89×10^9), shape variation gives a wider minimum-loss range (2.4346–2.5089) than at fixed N.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Parameter count is a better invariant than FLOPs/token for loss and hyperparameter optima across shapes.

fits_no_version.finding: Optimal peak learning rate follows 1.79 N^-0.713 D^0.307, and optimal batch size follows 0.58 D^0.571, largely independent of N.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal training hyperparameters scale as power laws in N and D.

record.problems: The relevant fixed-parameter result is reported as an aggregate range rather than per-architecture loss values. The tested architecture and scale range is limited; the paper notes that its findings are primarily data-driven.

untested.parts: Shape effects at other model sizes, wider aspect ratios (only 8–14 layers tested), and held-out rather than smooth training loss. Also the size of the shape effect when hyperparameters are not re-tuned per shape.
Not tested. Loss is reported at several N and D values but no loss power law is fitted.
Not tested for loss. Only hyperparameter optima are extrapolated.
Not tested for loss scaling. MoE and data-recipe results concern only hyperparameter prediction.
Not tested for loss exponents. The schedule effect (lrmin) is shown only on hyperparameter optima.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V4 reading is sound. The loss values are smooth training loss with tuned hyperparameters. The study's code is released, and the paper is a preprint.

versions.untested_parts: Loss scaling with parameter count, training tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation of loss power laws fitted on small runs to much larger runs.

rows.note: The paper describes the minimum-loss variation as minimal despite the architectural differences; the reported range aggregates the eight configurations.
rows.check: Link and state are correct. The measure is minimum smooth training loss, which the paper uses as a proxy for validation loss (Sec. 3.3.3), not held-out loss. The spread of about 0.048 (about 2%) covers only 8–14 layers at one scale. Per-shape minima are only partly readable from the garbled Fig. 6 heatmaps.
